questions.question: What are the essential Docker commands every developer should know?
questions.direct_answer: Essential Docker commands include docker build to create images from Dockerfiles, docker run to start containers, docker ps to list running containers, docker stop and docker rm to halt and remove containers, docker images to view local images, docker logs to read container output, and docker pull to download images from registries like Docker Hub.
follow_up_questions: How do you view the last 50 lines of container logs?
What does docker exec -it container bash allow you to do?

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **docker build**: creates immutable images from Dockerfiles — run this after every code change
**docker run**: starts new containers from images — use -d for background, -p for port mapping, --name for easy reference
**docker ps**: lists containers — add -a to see stopped ones, essential for debugging startup failures
**docker logs**: shows container stdout/stderr — use -f to follow in real time like tail -f
**docker exec**: runs commands inside running containers — docker exec -it container_name /bin/bash opens interactive shell

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I'd say the essential Docker commands break into three groups. First, for building and running, you've got docker build to create images from your Dockerfile and docker run to start containers from those images. When I'm developing a Spring Boot app, I use docker build after every code change and docker run with the -d flag to start it in the background. Second, for monitoring what's happening, there's docker ps to list running containers and docker logs to see application output. I always use docker logs -f to follow logs in real time when I'm testing new features. The -f flag is crucial because otherwise you're constantly rerunning the command. Third, for debugging and cleanup, docker exec lets you open a shell inside a running container — that's super helpful when logs aren't enough and you need to check if a file exists or test network connectivity. Then docker stop and docker rm handle shutdown and removal. One mistake I see a lot is people forgetting that images and containers are different — you can't docker rm an image, you need docker rmi for that. Also, it's worth knowing docker system prune to clean up disk space, because Docker caches everything and you can easily end up with 20 gigs of old images after a few weeks. The key is understanding the image-container relationship — images are like JAR files, containers are like running JVM processes.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Docker commands follow the object lifecycle. `docker pull` obtains an image, `docker build` creates one, and `docker image ls` lists local images. `docker run` is a convenience that creates and starts a container; `docker create` and `docker start` expose those stages separately.

Use `docker ps` for running containers and `docker ps -a` for all containers. `docker logs`, `docker inspect`, `docker stats`, and `docker exec` help diagnose a container. `docker stop`, `docker rm`, and `docker image rm` operate on different objects.

The important skill is not memorizing a long list: first decide whether you are working with an image, a container, a network, a volume, or a build cache, then use `--help` and inspect before any cleanup command.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Build and Run|~Create and start|docker build -t app .|docker run -p 8080:8080|-d for background
blue|Inspect|~See what's happening|docker ps (-a for all)|docker logs -f|docker exec -it bash
emerald|Cleanup|~Free space|docker stop and rm|docker rmi for images|docker system prune
violet|Mental Model|~Image vs container|image is the JAR file|container is the running JVM|rm vs rmi differ

sections.title: When You Need Each Command
sections.content:
Use **docker build** whenever you change application code or dependencies — every time you modify your Spring Boot app.

Use **docker run** to start fresh containers for testing or when configuration changes require a clean state.

Use **docker ps** constantly during development to verify containers started correctly and see their status.

Use **docker logs** immediately when something breaks — it's your first debugging step before diving deeper.

Use **docker exec** when logs aren't enough and you need to check filesystem contents, test network connectivity with curl, or run SQL queries against an embedded database.

Use **docker stop** and **docker rm** when you need to free ports or want to start with a clean configuration after testing.

Use **docker system prune** weekly to reclaim disk space consumed by old images and stopped containers.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing images and containers**: Freshers try docker rm on an image or docker rmi on a running container, getting cryptic errors. Remember images are templates, containers are instances — you can't remove a template while instances are using it.
- **Forgetting the -d flag in docker run**: Without detached mode, your terminal hangs and you can't run other commands. You end up with multiple terminal windows instead of running containers in the background.
- **Using docker ps without -a**: You only see running containers, so when your container crashes immediately after starting, docker ps shows nothing and you think Docker is broken. Always use docker ps -a to see stopped containers and their exit codes.

questions.question: What does docker run -p 8080:8080 mean?
questions.direct_answer: `docker run -p 8080:8080 IMAGE` publishes container TCP port 8080 on host port 8080. Without a host IP, Docker commonly binds the published port on all host addresses, not only localhost. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080` when the service should be reachable only from the host.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between EXPOSE in Dockerfile and -p in docker run?
How do you run a container and map port 80 on the host to port 8080 in the container?

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Syntax: `[host-ip:]host-port:container-port[/protocol]`.
- The right-hand port is where the process listens inside the container.
- The left-hand port is opened on the Docker host.
- Without an IP, the port is commonly published on all host interfaces and may be externally reachable.
- `EXPOSE` documents a port; `-p` publishes it.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The -p flag maps ports between your host machine and the container. The format is -p followed by host port, colon, container port. So -p 8080:8080 means when you hit localhost:8080 on your machine, Docker forwards that traffic to port 8080 inside the container. The reason you need this is that containers run in isolated networks — each container has its own private localhost. When your Spring Boot app starts in a container and listens on 8080, that's port 8080 in the container's network, not your machine's network. Without the -p flag, you can't reach it even though the container is running. A common pattern I use is -p 9090:8080 when I'm running multiple services and port 8080 is already taken by something else. The container still listens on 8080 internally, but I access it through 9090 on my host. That's really useful in microservices development. You can also map multiple ports with multiple -p flags, like -p 8080:8080 -p 5005:5005 if you want to attach a debugger to your containerized app. One mistake I see freshers make is forgetting the -p flag completely, then wondering why localhost:8080 doesn't work. The container is actually fine and listening, but it's in a separate network namespace. Another mistake is reversing the order — the host port always comes first, then the container port. It helps to think of it as traffic flowing from left to right, from your machine into the container.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A process in the container listens on a **container port**. Publishing creates a host-side listener and a forwarding rule to that container endpoint. In `-p 8080:8080`, the first 8080 is the host port and the second is the container port. They do not need to match: `-p 8081:8080` serves the same container on host port 8081.

The missing host address is important. Docker normally publishes on all host addresses, so saying 'localhost only' can expose a development service farther than intended. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080` for loopback-only access.

Publishing is different from Dockerfile `EXPOSE`, which supplies metadata and supports `-P` but does not itself create a host mapping. Also verify that the application listens on the container interface and expected port.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Port Mapping|~host colon container|-p 8080:8080|left is your machine|right is inside container
blue|Why Needed|~Containers are isolated|private network|-p punches a hole|EXPOSE is only docs
emerald|Patterns|~Flexible mapping|-p 9090:8080 avoids conflict|multiple -p flags|127.0.0.1 binds local
violet|Common Trap|~Forgot the -p|container runs fine|localhost refuses|nothing reachable

sections.title: When to Use Different Port Mapping Patterns
sections.content:
Use **-p 8080:8080** for standard development when you want the container port to match your usual local port — makes it easy to remember and switch between containerized and non-containerized setups.

Use **-p 9090:8080** when port 8080 is already occupied by another service or container — this happens constantly in microservices development when running multiple services simultaneously.

Use **multiple -p flags** like -p 8080:8080 -p 5005:5005 when your container exposes multiple ports — HTTP on 8080 plus a remote debugger on 5005 or a metrics endpoint on 9091.

Use **-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080** when the service should only be accessible from your local machine, not from the network — adds security for databases or admin interfaces.

Use **-p without host port** like -p 8080 to let Docker assign a random available port — useful in automated testing where you don't care about the specific port number.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the -p flag entirely**: Freshers run docker run without port mapping, see the container running with docker ps, then spend an hour debugging why localhost:8080 doesn't work. The container is fine — it's listening on 8080 inside its network — but that network is isolated from your host.
- **Reversing the port order**: Using -p 8080:9090 when you meant -p 9090:8080 leads to confusing errors. The pattern is always host first, container second. Remember the traffic flows from left to right: from your machine into the container.
- **Not checking for port conflicts**: Running docker run -p 8080:8080 when another container or local process already uses 8080 fails with a bind error. Use docker ps to see what's using ports, or use a different host port like 9090.

questions.question: How do you view logs from a running Docker container?
questions.direct_answer: Use docker logs followed by the container ID or name to see all output from a container. For example, docker logs order-api shows stdout and stderr. Add -f to follow logs in real time like tail -f, --tail 100 to see only the last 100 lines, and --since 10m to view logs from the last 10 minutes. Combine flags for targeted debugging.
follow_up_questions: Where does Docker store logs on the host machine?
How do you configure Spring Boot to write structured JSON logs in Docker?

sections.title: Reading Container Logs for Debugging
sections.content:
When you run a Spring Boot app locally, you see console output immediately in your terminal. With Docker, that output goes into the container's isolated environment.

The **docker logs** command retrieves stdout and stderr from a container and displays them on your host machine. You reference the container by name or ID: **docker logs order-api** or **docker logs a3f8b2c1**. By default, this dumps the entire log history and exits — fine for quick checks but impractical for debugging active issues. The **-f flag** (follow) works like tail -f, streaming new log lines as they appear. This is essential when testing API endpoints or watching for errors in real time. The **--tail N flag** shows only the last N lines, preventing your terminal from being flooded with thousands of startup messages. The **--since flag** filters by time: --since 10m shows logs from the last 10 minutes, --since 2023-12-01 shows everything after a specific date. Combining these flags creates powerful debugging workflows: **docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f order-api** follows recent logs without historical noise.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Basics|~Read app output|docker logs name|stdout and stderr|same as local console
blue|Live Follow|~The -f flag|streams new lines|like tail -f|daily debugging
emerald|Trim Output|~Focus on recent|--tail 100|--since 10m|combine flags
violet|Gotcha|~Logs must hit stdout|file appender means blank|configure stdout|crashed means no new lines

sections.title: Common Log Viewing Patterns
When to Use Each Log Command Pattern
sections.content:
Use **docker logs container_name** without flags for quick health checks — did the app start successfully, are there any obvious errors in recent output.

Use **docker logs -f** during active development when testing new features or API endpoints — you need to see responses and errors as they happen, just like watching console output in local development.

Use **docker logs --tail 50** when you suspect a recent error but don't want to scroll through hundreds of startup log lines — Spring Boot initialization is verbose and you care about what happened in the last few seconds.

Use **docker logs --since 10m** when investigating an issue reported at a specific time — a user complained 5 minutes ago, so you check logs from that timeframe.

Use **docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f** as your standard debugging command — start with recent logs, then follow new ones, avoiding historical noise.

Use **docker logs container_name | grep ERROR** to scan for exceptions across all output when you don't know when the problem occurred.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not using -f for real-time debugging**: Freshers run docker logs repeatedly in a loop, hitting up-arrow and Enter, missing events between executions. Using -f keeps the stream open so you see every log line as it happens — critical when testing API calls or watching for specific errors.
- **Overwhelming the terminal with historical logs**: Running docker logs without --tail on a container that's been running for hours dumps thousands of lines, making it impossible to find recent errors. Always use --tail or --since to limit output.
- **Forgetting containers stop writing logs after exit**: If the container crashed, docker logs shows output up to the crash, but no new lines appear even with -f. Check docker ps -a to see if the container exited, then read logs to find the cause.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **docker logs container_name**: shows all stdout and stderr from the container — your primary debugging tool
**-f flag**: follows logs in real time like tail -f — essential during active development and testing
**--tail N**: limits output to last N lines — prevents terminal flooding from verbose Spring Boot startup logs
**--since**: filters by time — --since 10m shows last 10 minutes, --since 2h shows last 2 hours
**Combining flags**: docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f gives targeted real-time debugging without historical noise

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To view logs from a running Docker container, you use the docker logs command followed by the container name or ID. So if my container is called order-api, I'd run docker logs order-api. That shows all the output — everything your Spring Boot app wrote to stdout and stderr. But in practice, I almost always use the -f flag to follow logs in real time, like docker logs -f order-api. That's crucial during development because you want to see what happens when you call an API endpoint or trigger some feature. Without -f, you're constantly rerunning the command and missing events between executions. Now, if the container has been running for a while, docker logs dumps thousands of lines and you can't find anything useful. That's where --tail comes in. I use docker logs --tail 50 order-api to see just the last 50 lines, which skips all the Spring Boot startup noise and shows recent activity. Another really helpful flag is --since for filtering by time. Like docker logs --since 10m shows logs from the last 10 minutes. I combine these when debugging: docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 -f order-api. That starts with the last 100 lines from the last 5 minutes, then follows new output. It's perfect for investigating an error that just happened without scrolling through historical logs. One thing freshers forget is that once a container stops, logs stop too. If you're using -f and nothing appears, check docker ps -a to see if the container crashed. Then run docker logs without -f to see what happened before it died.

questions.question: How do you clean up Docker resources (stopped containers, unused images)?
questions.direct_answer: Start with `docker system df`, then remove only confirmed unused objects. `docker container prune` removes stopped containers; `docker image prune` removes dangling images by default (`-a` broadens it); `docker network prune` removes unused networks; and build-cache/volume cleanup is separate. `docker system prune` combines several categories but does not remove named volumes unless explicitly requested.
follow_up_questions: What is a dangling image in Docker?
How do you automatically remove a container when it stops?

sections.title: Managing Docker Disk Usage
sections.content:
Docker consumes disk space aggressively through **layer caching**. Every time you run docker build, Docker saves intermediate layers so future builds reuse them — this speeds up builds dramatically but accumulates gigabytes of data. **Stopped containers** persist on disk even after you stop them, storing their entire filesystem state in case you want to restart or inspect them. **Dangling images** are layers that aren't tagged and aren't referenced by any container — they're leftovers from rebuilds when you reuse the same tag. After a few weeks of development, you can easily hit 20-30 GB of Docker data without realizing it. The **docker system prune** command is the nuclear option: it removes all stopped containers, all networks not used by at least one container, all dangling images, and all dangling build cache. For surgical cleanup, **docker container prune** removes only stopped containers, and **docker image prune** removes only unused images. Use **docker system df** to see how much space Docker consumes before deciding what to clean.

The key is understanding that Docker prioritizes performance through caching — it never automatically deletes anything.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Why It Grows|~Docker caches all|build layers pile up|stopped containers stay|20-plus GB in weeks
blue|Check First|~Measure usage|docker system df|images, containers, cache|decide what to cut
emerald|Targeted|~Surgical cleanup|container prune|image prune|rm and rmi specifics
violet|Nuclear|~Broad sweep|system prune|-a removes unused images|careful in prod

sections.title: Docker Cleanup Commands
When to Use Each Cleanup Command
sections.content:
Use **docker system df** weekly or when disk space warnings appear — it shows how much space Docker consumes across images, containers, volumes, and build cache, helping you decide what to clean.

Use **docker system prune** as routine maintenance every few weeks during active development — it reclaims space from stopped test containers and dangling layers without affecting your current work.

Use **docker system prune -a** when disk space is critically low or before major version upgrades — this removes all unused images, not just dangling ones, so you'll need to rebuild or re-pull images on next use.

Use **docker container prune** when you've been running lots of temporary test containers and want to keep your image cache intact.

Use **docker image prune** when you've rebuilt the same image many times and know old versions are safe to delete.

Use **docker rm** and **docker rmi** for targeted deletion of specific containers or images during debugging when you want precise control.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing Docker caches everything**: Freshers run docker build dozens of times during a feature, never realizing that each failed build leaves layers behind. Weeks later, Docker uses 25GB and they think it's a bug. Running docker system df reveals the truth — build cache alone can hit 15GB.
- **Confusing docker rm and docker rmi**: Trying to delete an image with docker rm order-service:v1 fails with a confusing error. Remember: rm for containers (running instances), rmi for images (templates). The names are frustratingly similar.
- **Pruning without checking first**: Running docker system prune -a blindly deletes all unused images, forcing you to rebuild or re-download everything on next use. Always run docker system df first to see what you're about to delete and whether it's worth the rebuild cost.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Inspect first with `docker system df` and object-list commands.
- `docker container prune` removes stopped containers.
- `docker image prune` removes dangling images; `-a` includes images unused by any container.
- `docker system prune` also considers unused networks and build cache, but volumes need an explicit option/separate command.
- Prune commands can remove caches or data you expected to keep; read the candidate list and flags.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I start cleanup by running `docker system df` and listing containers, images, volumes, and build cache so I know what owns the space. Then I choose the narrowest command.

`docker container prune` removes stopped containers. `docker image prune` removes dangling images by default; `docker image prune -a` also removes images unused by any container. `docker network prune` removes unused networks, and build cache and volumes have separate prune commands. `docker system prune` combines several categories, but named volumes are not removed by default.

The key safety point is that 'unused' is Docker's reference test, not my business-retention intent. A stopped debugging container, cached image for rollback, anonymous volume, or build cache may still be valuable. I inspect filters and the confirmation list, back up data, and avoid broad scheduled prune commands on shared production hosts without a retention policy.

questions.question: How do you debug a running Docker container — what commands do you use?
questions.title: Debugging a Running Docker Container
questions.direct_answer: Begin with `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `docker inspect`, `docker stats`, and application health checks. Use `docker exec -it <container> sh` only if the image contains a shell and policy permits it; minimal/distroless images may not. Inspect configuration carefully because environment output can contain secrets, and reproduce long investigations from the image/Dockerfile rather than changing a running container.

sections.title: Debugging Running Containers
sections.content:
Debugging containerized applications requires different tools than local development. You can't just open a file explorer or attach a debugger with one click — containers are isolated environments.

The **docker logs** command is your first stop: it shows stdout and stderr, revealing startup errors, exceptions, and application output. But logs only tell part of the story. Sometimes you need to see if a configuration file exists, check network connectivity, or verify environment variables. That's where **docker exec** comes in. Running **docker exec -it container_name sh (when the image contains a shell)** opens an interactive shell inside the running container, giving you full access to the filesystem and tools like curl, ls, cat, and env. You're literally inside the container's namespace, seeing exactly what the application sees. For configuration inspection, **docker inspect** dumps a massive JSON object containing everything about the container: environment variables, port mappings, volume mounts, network settings, and resource limits. This is crucial when your app behaves differently in Docker versus locally — often the issue is a missing environment variable or incorrect volume mount. Advanced debugging includes **docker stats** for real-time CPU and memory usage, and **docker top** to see running processes inside the container.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|docker logs|~First stop|-f to follow|--tail to trim|shows stack traces
blue|docker exec -it|~Get inside|open a /bin/bash shell|check files, env, curl|-i stdin, -t tty
emerald|docker inspect|~Config as JSON|env vars and ports|volumes and network|local vs Docker diffs
violet|Performance|~Resource view|docker stats|live CPU and memory|docker top processes

sections.title: Container Debugging Workflow
When to Use Each Debugging Command
sections.content:
Use **docker logs -f** as your first debugging step for any issue — if the app throws exceptions or fails to start, logs reveal the problem 80% of the time.

Use **docker exec -it container_name sh (when the image contains a shell)** when logs aren't enough and you need to verify filesystem state — check if a configuration file got copied into the image, see if the application JAR exists in the right location, or test network connectivity with curl to other services.

Use **docker inspect** when behavior differs between local and Docker environments — the issue is often a missing environment variable, incorrect port mapping, or volume mount pointing to the wrong path.

Use **docker stats** when the app runs but performs poorly — shows real-time CPU and memory usage, revealing if you're hitting container resource limits or if the JVM is consuming unexpected memory.

Use **docker top** to see what processes are actually running inside the container — useful when a shell script launches multiple processes and you need to verify they're all alive.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only using docker logs**: Freshers stop at logs and give up when the error isn't obvious. They don't realize they can open a shell with docker exec and poke around inside the container to check files, test commands, or verify configuration.
- **Forgetting -it flags on docker exec**: Running docker exec without -i -t results in non-interactive or missing terminal output. The -it combination is essential — -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a pseudo-TTY for proper terminal behavior.
- **Not having debugging tools in the image**: Opening a shell with docker exec only to find curl, wget, and even ls are missing because the base image is Alpine or a distroless variant. Production images strip unnecessary tools, but during debugging you need them — either use a different base image for dev or install tools temporarily.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Confirm state and exit code with `docker ps -a` and `docker inspect`.
- Read stdout/stderr with `docker logs --tail ...`; logging drivers can change availability.
- Check resource use with `docker stats` and health with the application's endpoint.
- Use `docker exec` only when a suitable executable exists; `/bin/bash` is not guaranteed.
- Treat in-container edits as temporary evidence, not the production fix; avoid printing secrets.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I debug a running container from the outside in. First I check `docker ps -a` for state, restart count, and exit status. Then I read a bounded log window with `docker logs --tail 200 <name>` and inspect health, mounts, networks, published ports, and configured limits with `docker inspect`. `docker stats` shows live resource pressure.

If the image contains diagnostic tools and policy allows it, I can run `docker exec -it <name> sh` and inspect processes or connectivity. I do not assume `/bin/bash` exists—distroless images may have no shell—and I avoid dumping environment values that can contain secrets.

For a crash-loop or already exited process, logs and inspect are usually more useful than exec. Any manual change inside a running container is temporary evidence, not the fix. I reproduce the issue in the Dockerfile/configuration, rebuild the image, and verify the replacement container.
